ai.title: Thoracic Vertebrae Anatomy
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The twelve thoracic vertebrae form the middle spine, articulate with ribs, and protect the spinal cord. Understanding their landmarks aids diagnosis of trauma and spinal disease in low‑resource settings.

b: T1 is unique: small body, long spinous process, and a full rib facet.
T12 resembles lumbar vertebrae: larger body, no rib facets.
sections.p: The thoracic spine consists of twelve vertebrae (T1‑T12) that bridge the cervical and lumbar regions. Each vertebra has a body, vertebral arch, transverse processes with costal facets, and a spinous process that slopes inferiorly.

b: Body size increases from T1 to T12.
Pedicles are short and angled, creating a narrow canal.
sections.p: Thoracic vertebrae lie posterior to the thoracic cavity, at the level of the ribs. The vertebral foramen houses the spinal cord, which ends at L1‑L2.

b: The aorta lies to the left of T4‑T12.
sections.p: Anteriorly the vertebral bodies contact the posterior mediastinum and great vessels. Posteriorly the spinous processes are palpable in the mid‑line. Lateral transverse processes articulate with rib heads.

b: Anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two‑thirds of the cord.
Posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns.
sections.p: Segmental spinal arteries (posterior intercostal arteries) arise from the aorta and supply the vertebral bodies and posterior elements.

b: T1 contributes to the brachial plexus (C8‑T1).
T2‑T12 supply the thoracic wall and abdominal wall.
sections.p: The spinal cord exits via intervertebral foramina as thoracic spinal nerves (T1‑T12). These form the intercostal nerves that run along the inferior border of each rib.

b: Limited forward flexion protects the cord.
Rotation is minimal compared with cervical spine.
sections.p: Provides attachment for ribs, limits flexion, and protects the spinal cord. The kyphotic curve distributes axial load and aids respiration by allowing rib movement.

b: Burst fracture: vertebral body fragments may impinge the canal.
Flexion‑distraction (Chance) injury: horizontal fracture through pedicles, common in seat‑belt injuries.
sections.p: Thoracic vertebral fractures often result from high‑energy trauma or osteoporosis. Compression, burst, and flexion‑distraction patterns each have distinct radiographic signs and management pathways.

t.b: Detects gross fracture, vertebral height loss, and associated rib fractures; if unavailable, use bedside ultrasound for vertebral step‑offs.
Defines fracture pattern and canal compromise; if CT unavailable, rely on clinical neuro exam and plain films.
Assesses cord edema, ligamentous injury, and epidural hematoma; if MRI unavailable, monitor for progressive neurological deficit.

b: Paraspinal muscle spasm indicates acute injury.
Sensory level on trunk points to cord involvement.
sections.p: At the bedside, assess for midline tenderness, step‑off, and neurological deficits. Palpate spinous processes from C7 to L5; a palpable step at T12 suggests a fracture.

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive motor weakness below the level of injury
Severe respiratory compromise from high thoracic injury
